questions.lessonTitle: Base Model Selection for Domain-Specific Pretraining
questions.lessonContent: Composer 2's continued pretraining stage extends Kimi K2.5, a 1.04T parameter / 32B active parameter Mixture-of-Experts model. The selection process evaluated three potential open-source base models: GLM-5, Kimi K2.5, and DeepSeek V3.2. Three internal evaluations contributed to this selection: FreshBench for coding knowledge (where higher scores are better), an internal State Tracking benchmark similar to LoCoDiff that measures average character-level distance (where lower scores are better), and codebase perplexity measured as the sum of negative log-likelihoods over a rolling window on their private monorepo (where lower scores are better). Kimi K2.5 achieved 83.2% on FreshBench, 86 on State Tracking, and 13.81M negative log-likelihood. Kimi K2.5 was chosen due to general strong performance and infrastructure efficiency considerations.

questions.lessonTitle: Continued Pretraining Data Mix and Phases
questions.lessonContent: Composer 2's continued pretraining stage extends Kimi K2.5 with a large code-dominated data mix and is divided into three phases. The bulk of compute is spent at 32k token sequence length, followed by a shorter long-context extension phase to 256k sequence length, and finally a short SFT phase on targeted coding tasks. Multi-Token Prediction layers are trained atop a checkpoint cut from the middle of the continued pretraining run, and during the final two phases (long-context and SFT), the MTP layers are included and trained jointly with the rest of the model.

questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 uses Context Parallelism as the primary long-context scaling axis, requiring less communication than Tensor Parallelism and improving compute efficiency by preserving full hidden dimensions. For the continued pretraining phase, Expert Parallelism is set to 8 and Context Parallelism is set to 2 (EP=8, CP=2). For the RL phase, both values are increased to 8 (EP=8, CP=8). This decoupling of EP from TP enables support for larger expert-parallel degrees and makes expert-grouped GEMMs more efficient with larger per-rank token batches.

questions.moduleTitle: Reinforcement Learning for Agentic Code Generation
questions.lessonContent: To enable Composer 2 to work across long horizons during RL training, the team uses the self-summarization technique introduced in Composer 1.5. Each training rollout can involve multiple generations chained together by summaries, rather than a single prompt–response pair. The final reward is used for all tokens produced by the model in the chain. This upweights both the agent responses in good trajectories and also the self-summarizations that made them work, while poor summaries that lose critical information are downweighted. As Composer trains, it learns to use self-summaries to process more information, even with a limited context window. For hard examples, it often self-summarizes multiple times. Experiments found that self-summary consistently reduces error compared to using separate prompt-based compaction, while using significantly fewer tokens and reusing the KV cache.

questions.moduleTitle: Reinforcement Learning for Agentic Code Generation
questions.lessonTitle: KL Divergence Estimator Selection in RL
questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 uses a Kullback–Leibler divergence for regularization during RL training, formulated as KL(q ∥ p) = E_{x∼q}[−log r(x)], where r(x) = p(x)/q(x). Many open-source implementations estimate KL with the estimator k3 = (r−1) − log r, defined in Schulman's prior work. The k3 estimator is unbiased and reduces variance when p and q are close. However, Amini et al. showed that the variance of k3 increases drastically as p and q diverge. In contrast, the k2 estimator does not suffer from variance blow-up but is biased. For large KL values, the variance of the k3 estimate becomes extremely large. Therefore, Composer 2 explicitly uses the standard estimator k1 = −log r instead. Figure 4 in the report visualizes this comparison between estimators.
questions.question: Which KL divergence estimator does Composer 2 use for regularization, and why was this choice made over alternatives?
choices: No KL regularization is used in Composer 2's RL training
k1 = −log r, because k3 suffers from extreme variance blow-up when p and q diverge
k2, because it provides unbiased estimation with minimal variance
k3 = (r−1) − log r, because it reduces variance when distributions are close
questions.explanation: The k3 estimator, while unbiased and variance-reducing for close distributions, has drastically increased variance when p and q diverge. The k2 estimator avoids variance blow-up but is biased. The standard k1 = −log r estimator was chosen to avoid the variance issues of k3.

correctness.explanation: The source content explicitly states that the k3 estimator (r-1) - log r has drastically increased variance when p and q diverge, and that the k1 = -log r estimator is used instead to avoid these variance issues.

questions.lessonTitle: Reinforcement Learning for Agentic Code Generation
questions.lessonContent: Composer 2's reinforcement learning training follows a specific sequence to improve end-to-end coding performance. The process begins with sampling a problem from the training distribution. Next, the system simulates rollouts, generating multiple solution trajectories with different approaches. Finally, model weights are updated based on the quality of these solutions through policy gradient learning. This three-step core loop—sampling problems, simulating rollouts, and updating weights—drives the model's improvement in reasoning, multi-step execution, and long-horizon coherence.

questions.lessonContent: Stateful codebase environments are a first-class artifact of Composer 2's post-training stack. Environments run on Anyrun, an internal compute platform built for running untrusted code at scale, which also powers Cloud Agents and Automations in the Cursor product. Each pod in Anyrun is a dedicated Firecracker VM capable of running a full development environment, including a browser and GUI for computer use. Anyrun supports forking and snapshotting of full coding environments at both the filesystem and memory level, enabling mid-trajectory rollout checkpointing and post-rollout state capture. Each Anyrun cluster can schedule more than 500 pods per second.

questions.lessonContent: Every training step, Composer 2 synchronizes updated weights to the inference engine by uploading to a shared S3 bucket. To minimize transfer size, delta compression is used: each rank caches its previous upload and transmits only the diff against the new weights. Because RL updates are small, even with full-parameter training these diffs compress to a handful of gigabytes for the 1T-parameter model. Uploading is fully sharded across all training ranks, allowing saturation of the egress bandwidth. During training, inference ran across geographically distributed clusters in the US and Europe, with each cluster independently downloading and reconstructing weights.
